newsitem.title: USA: COMEX copper ends lower, more Sumitomo sales seen.
newsitem.headline: COMEX copper ends lower, more Sumitomo sales seen.

text.p: COMEX front month copper futures ended lower Monday, after comments by Canadian scrap merchant, Herbert Black suggesting Sumitomo may still have "several hundred thousand tonnes of copper to liquidate", traders said.
COMEX December copper ended down 0.70 cent at 88.45 cents midday, after trading in a 90.10-88.30 cent range.
Black, who appeared on U.S. television during the Sumitomo crisis mid-year to announce he had made large profits shorting copper, said copper could fall to $1,600 a tonne in 1997.
Black was speaking at an LME week luncheon in London.
LME three month copper ended lower at $1905.00 a tonne in London.
LME copper stocks remain relatively low at 229,575 tonnes, helping to widen the backwardation in both LME and COMEX copper, traders said.

"Copper remains hemmed in by technical trading strategies and prices are expected to fluctuate within recent objectives of 84 cents on the downside and $1.00 on the upside in the near term," CPM Group analyst Edward Kemp said.
Monday's weakness merely took December copper back down to near support provided by the uptrend in COMEX December copper from three month lows seen in early September at 84.50 cents, traders said.

But Bloomsbury Mineral Economics in London calculates there will probably be a global copper supply surplus of around 175,000 tonnes in the second half of 1996, while in 1997 the surplus could rise to 250,000-300,000 tonnes, analysts noted.

"As more production builds up during 1998, it is quite possible for prices to go as low as $1,653 to 1,553 a tonne (75 to 70 cents a lb basis Comex)," Merrill Lynch analyst Ted Arnold said in a weekly report.
